import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 931

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/931](https://www.erdosproblems.com/931)
-/

namespace Erdos931

/--
Let $k_1 \geq k_2 \geq 3$. Are there only finitely many $n_2\geq n_1 + k_1$
such that
$$
  \prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(n_1 + i)\ \text{and}\ \prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2} (n_2 + j)
$$
have the same prime factors?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (k₁ : ℕ) (k₂ ≥ 3), k₂ ≤ k₁ →
    { (n₁, n₂) | n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂ ∧
      (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors }.Finite := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős thought perhaps if the two products have the same factors then
$n_2 > 2(n_1 + k_1)$.
It is an open question whether this is true when allowing a finite number of counterexamples.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931.variants.additional_condition : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (k₁ : ℕ) (k₂ ≥ 3), k₂ ≤ k₁ →
    {(n₁, n₂) | n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂ ∧ n₂ ≤ 2 * (n₁ + k₁) ∧
      (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors}.Finite := by
  sorry

/--
In fact there exist counterexamples, like this one found by AlphaProof.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931.variants.additional_condition_nonempty : ∃ (k₁ k₂ : ℕ), ∃ (_h₁ : k₂ ≤ k₁), ∃ (_h₂ : 3 ≤ k₂),
  {(n₁, n₂) | n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂ ∧ n₂ ≤ 2 * (n₁ + k₁) ∧
      (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors}.Nonempty := by
  use 10, 3, (by norm_num), (by norm_num)
  use (0, 13)
  norm_num [Finset.prod_Icc_succ_top]
  norm_num +decide [Nat.primeFactors, Nat.primeFactorsList]

/--
Erdős was unable to prove that if the two products have the same factors
then there must exist a prime between $n_1$ and $n_2$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_931.variants.exists_prime (k₁ k₂ n₁ n₂ : ℕ) (h₁ : k₂ ≤ k₁) (h₂ : 3 ≤ k₂)
    (h₃ : n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂) (h₄ : (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors) :
    ∃ (p : ℕ), p.Prime ∧ n₁ ≤ p ∧ p ≤ n₂ := by
  sorry

end Erdos931

reformulations.difference: The source asks for finitely many admissible n₂, whereas Lean asserts finiteness of the set of admissible pairs (n₁,n₂).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Projection onto n₂ sends a finite pair set to a finite set. Conversely, n₁+k₁≤n₂ implies n₁≤n₂, so a bound N on the admissible n₂ bounds both coordinates of every admissible pair. The pair set is therefore contained in {0,…,N}². This equivalence was proved for an arbitrary additional predicate in Review931.finite_pairs_iff_finite_second.

reformulations.difference: Lean expresses the finite-exception version of n₂>2(n₁+k₁) by requiring the set of violating pairs to be finite.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A violation of the strict bound is exactly n₂≤2(n₁+k₁). For fixed lengths, finiteness of the displayed bad-pair set is equivalent to the existence of N such that every admissible pair with n₂>N satisfies the strict bound. The converse uses n₁≤n₂ to bound both coordinates of exceptions. This equivalence was proved in Review931.finite_bad_iff_eventual_ratio.

reformulations.difference: The original paper describes impossibility of equal prime-factor sets when both starting points lie strictly between the same two consecutive primes. Lean instead concludes that a prime lies in the closed interval [n₁,n₂].
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Under the problem's standing hypotheses, n₁≤n₂ and n₂≥3. Having no prime in [n₁,n₂] is equivalent to the existence of consecutive primes p<q with p<n₁≤n₂<q: choose the preceding and following primes. The small cases before the first prime cannot cause an exception, since 2 lies in [n₁,n₂] whenever n₁≤2. Contraposing the prime-gap assertion therefore gives exactly the closed-interval conclusion, including its non-strict endpoints. The pointwise equivalence, specialized to the file's prime-factor predicate and parameter hypotheses, was proved in /workspace/review/primegap.lean.

review.notes: All four declarations were checked. The source still marks problem 931 open and records the counterexample to the unqualified ratio bound. Nat.primeFactors has the intended multiplicity-free meaning; Lean proofs confirm that all relevant products are positive and greater than one, excluding its exceptional values at 0 and 1. The explicit counterexample has prime-factor set {2,3,5,7}, and its proof has no sorryAx dependency. Small-input tests also verify satisfiable hypotheses at k₁=k₂=3 and Tijdeman's example. The equivalence and boundary-check files in /workspace/review/ compile successfully without sorryAx. Full access to Guy's §B35 was unavailable; the cited problem page and original Erdős paper sufficed to verify the declarations. The reviewed file's hash matches the specified commit. Pre-existing sandbox changes to lakefile.toml and run/ were left untouched.
